questions.stem: Why is Iago angry with Othello at the start of the play?
options: Othello has dismissed Iago from the army for drinking
Othello has made Cassio his lieutenant instead of Iago
Othello has refused to pay Iago for his years of service
Othello has chosen Roderigo as his lieutenant over Iago
questions.explanation: Iago, Othello's ensign, complains to Roderigo that Cassio, a Florentine who has 'never set a squadron in the field', got the promotion. He says he follows Othello only 'to serve my turn upon him.'

questions.stem: How does Brabantio learn that his daughter has married Othello?
options: Cassio comes to his house to invite him to the wedding feast
Iago and Roderigo wake him at night, shouting the news below his window
Desdemona writes him a long letter from Cyprus explaining what she has done
The Duke tells him when the Senate meets to discuss the Turkish fleet
questions.explanation: Iago stays hidden in the dark and uses crude, racist images to enrage Brabantio. From the first scene he works by provoking others while keeping out of sight.

questions.stem: What does Brabantio accuse Othello of in front of the Senate?
options: Forcing Desdemona to marry him against her will
Using witchcraft or drugs to win Desdemona's love
Stealing his fortune to pay for the war in Cyprus
Planning to betray Venice to the Turkish fleet
questions.explanation: Brabantio cannot believe his daughter chose Othello freely. Othello explains that she fell in love with the stories of his life, and Desdemona confirms it.

questions.stem: Why are Othello, Desdemona and the others sent to Cyprus?
options: The Duke wants Othello to marry Desdemona far from her angry father
Cassio has been made governor and has asked Othello to help him rule
A Turkish fleet is threatening the island, and Othello is sent to defend it
Othello has been exiled from Venice for marrying without Brabantio's consent
questions.explanation: Venice needs its best general against the Ottoman Turks. A storm destroys the Turkish fleet, so the war is over, leaving the characters on an isolated island with nothing to fight but each other.

questions.stem: How does Cassio lose his position as lieutenant?
options: Iago gets him drunk, he fights Roderigo and wounds Montano, and Othello dismisses him
Iago tells Othello that Cassio has stolen army funds to buy gifts for Desdemona
Cassio refuses an order to attack the Turkish fleet during the storm at sea
Cassio admits to Othello that he has been meeting Desdemona in secret
questions.explanation: Iago knows Cassio has a weak head for drink. In the brawl that follows, Othello tells Cassio, 'never more be officer of mine', exactly as Iago planned.

questions.stem: What advice does Iago give the disgraced Cassio?
options: To ask Desdemona to plead with Othello for him
To leave Cyprus before Othello can punish him
To challenge Roderigo to a duel to clear his name
To ask Montano to speak to Othello on his behalf
questions.explanation: It sounds like kind advice. In soliloquy, Iago reveals the trap: the more Desdemona pleads for Cassio, the more Othello will suspect her.

questions.stem: How does Iago get Desdemona's handkerchief?
options: He steals it from Desdemona's room while she is at the welcome feast
Cassio finds it and gives it to Iago to return to Othello
Bianca finds it in Cassio's room and sells it to Iago
Desdemona drops it, and Emilia picks it up and gives it to him
questions.explanation: When Othello says he has a pain in his forehead, Desdemona offers to bind it with the handkerchief, and it falls. Emilia knows Iago has often asked her to steal it, and gives it to him.

questions.stem: What does Iago do with the handkerchief?
options: Hands it to Othello, saying he took it from Cassio's own hand
Hides it in Emilia's room so that Othello will suspect his own wife
Shows it to Lodovico as proof that Desdemona has been unfaithful
Leaves it in Cassio's lodging, where Cassio finds it and gives it to Bianca
questions.explanation: Cassio, not knowing whose it is, asks Bianca to copy the embroidery. Later Othello sees it in Bianca's hands, and the 'trifle' becomes his proof.

questions.stem: In Act 4, Scene 1, Othello hides and watches Iago talking with Cassio. What does Othello think he sees?
options: Cassio returning the handkerchief to Iago and asking him to keep quiet
Cassio asking Iago to help him leave Cyprus with Desdemona that night
Cassio laughing about Desdemona, when he is really laughing about Bianca
Cassio confessing to Iago that he wants to murder Othello and rule Cyprus
questions.explanation: Othello cannot hear the words, only see Cassio's mocking laughter. Iago controls what Othello sees and how he reads it, a clear example of dramatic irony.

questions.stem: What shocks Lodovico, the visitor from Venice, in Act 4, Scene 1?
options: Othello refuses to obey the Duke's letter
Othello names Iago governor of Cyprus
Othello challenges Cassio to a duel
Othello strikes Desdemona in public
questions.explanation: Lodovico has known Othello as a noble, self-controlled general. Seeing him hit his wife, he asks whether this is the man the Senate trusted, which shows how far Iago has changed him.

questions.stem: How does Othello kill Desdemona?
options: He gives her a poisoned drink
He orders Iago to kill her
He smothers her in their bed
He stabs her with his sword
questions.explanation: Othello says he will not 'shed her blood'. He smothers her, still believing he is carrying out justice. She revives long enough to try to protect him.

questions.stem: How is the truth finally revealed in Act 5, Scene 2?
options: Bianca tells Lodovico that Iago paid her to lie about Cassio
Emilia says she found the handkerchief and gave it to Iago
Cassio produces a letter written by Iago before the murder
Roderigo confesses to Othello as he dies in Desdemona's room
questions.explanation: Emilia refuses to be silent even when Iago orders her home. When she tells the truth about the handkerchief, Iago kills her. Letters found on Roderigo confirm the plot.

questions.stem: How does the play end for Othello?
options: He is pardoned by Lodovico and allowed to remain governor of Cyprus
He stabs himself after a final speech asking to be remembered truly
He is taken back to Venice in chains to be tried before the Senate
He wounds Iago and is then killed by Lodovico's guards as he resists
questions.explanation: Othello asks to be described as one 'that loved not wisely, but too well', then kills himself and dies on a kiss. Cassio is left to rule Cyprus and to decide Iago's punishment.

questions.stem: Who is Roderigo?
options: A Venetian senator who supports Brabantio's charge of witchcraft
A wealthy Venetian, in love with Desdemona, whose money Iago takes
Desdemona's cousin, who carries messages between her and her father
Othello's servant, who has been with him since his days as a slave
questions.explanation: Iago tells him to 'Put money in thy purse', promising to win him Desdemona. 'Thus do I ever make my fool my purse,' Iago says, and later he kills Roderigo to silence him.

questions.stem: How does Othello behave in Act 1, Scene 2, when Brabantio's armed men come for him?
options: He stays calm and dignified, trusting his record to speak for him
He draws his sword at once and wounds two of Brabantio's servants
He agrees to go to prison until the Senate can hear Brabantio's case
He blames Desdemona and offers to send her home to her father
questions.explanation: 'Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them,' he says. His calm authority at the start makes his later collapse into jealousy and violence all the more terrible.

questions.stem: Why do critics disagree about Iago's motives?
options: He is given no soliloquies, so his reasons are left to the actor who plays him
He explains at the end that Othello once wronged his family, which resolves the question
He confesses to Lodovico that he loves Desdemona, which changes the meaning of the play
He gives several reasons, such as the promotion and a rumour about Emilia, but none seems enough
questions.explanation: Iago mentions losing the lieutenancy and a rumour that Othello slept with Emilia, but his reasons keep shifting. Coleridge called it 'motive-hunting', and Iago's final silence, 'Demand me nothing', keeps the question open.

questions.stem: What is Emilia's role in the final scene?
options: She persuades Othello to spare Iago so that he can stand trial in Venice
She exposes Iago's lies and defends Desdemona, though it costs her life
She helps Iago escape from the castle before the guards can arrest him
She confesses that she made up the story about Cassio to please Iago
questions.explanation: Emilia, Iago's wife, unknowingly helped him by taking the handkerchief. At the end she will not obey him and tells the truth, insisting her mistress 'was heavenly true'.

questions.stem: When the dying Desdemona is asked who killed her, she answers, 'Nobody. I myself. Farewell.' What does this show?
options: Her wish to blame Emilia for the lost handkerchief
Her loyal love for Othello, even as he wrongs her
Her guilt about the affair she had with Cassio
Her belief that Iago will be punished in time
questions.explanation: Desdemona protects Othello with her last words. Her faithfulness makes his mistake more tragic, and Othello's reply, calling her a liar, shows how blind he still is.

questions.stem: How does Cassio differ from Iago?
options: He is a hardened soldier with years of battle, while Iago is a bookish scholar
He is secretly plotting against Othello, while Iago is loyal to his general
He is coarse and cynical about women, while Iago is courtly and polite
He is courteous and honourable but careless, while Iago is controlled and deceitful
questions.explanation: Cassio is polite, especially to women, and weak with drink. Iago turns those qualities into weapons, making Cassio's charm look like a sign of an affair.

questions.stem: Why is it significant that Othello is a Moor serving the Venetian state?
options: He is distrusted by the Senate, which refuses him any command
He is valued as a general but remains an outsider in Venetian society
He is a Venetian noble by birth and is treated like any other senator
He is a prisoner of war forced to fight for Venice against his will
questions.explanation: The Senate needs Othello's military skill, but Brabantio, Iago and Roderigo show the prejudice he faces. His status as an outsider is something Iago exploits, and something Othello comes to doubt himself.

questions.stem: Iago, Roderigo and Brabantio use racist language about Othello. What is the effect on the audience?
options: It shows that the whole of Venice, including the Duke, agrees with Iago's view of Othello
It is meant to make the audience take Iago's side from the opening scene
It shows that Othello already accepts these views of himself from the opening scene
It reveals the speakers' prejudice before we meet Othello, who then proves them wrong
questions.explanation: In the first scene the audience hears Othello described in animal images before he appears. When he enters, calm and eloquent, the gap between the slander and the man exposes his accusers.

questions.stem: Why does Brabantio feel so wronged by his daughter's marriage?
options: He had already promised her in marriage to Roderigo
He expected to control whom she married, as fathers then did
He had already promised her to the Duke's son in a marriage contract
He had arranged for her to enter a convent outside Venice
questions.explanation: In Shakespeare's time a daughter was expected to marry with her father's consent. Desdemona speaks of a 'divided duty' between father and husband, and chooses Othello.

questions.stem: Who were the enemy that Venice feared would take Cyprus?
options: The Spanish navy
The French army
The English fleet
The Ottoman Turks
questions.explanation: In the late 1500s the Ottoman Empire was the great Mediterranean power and seized Cyprus from Venice in 1571. Venice's fear of 'the Turk' gives Othello his importance in Act 1.

questions.stem: Which theme is most central to Othello?
options: Jealousy and how it destroys trust and judgement
Ambition and the struggle to seize a throne
The rewards of loyalty in a just society
The corrupting effect of political power on rulers
questions.explanation: Iago calls jealousy 'the green-eyed monster'. Once Othello begins to suspect, he reads everything, even a handkerchief, as proof.

questions.stem: Why is the repeated phrase 'honest Iago' so important?
options: Iago serves as the play's moral voice, warning the others of danger
Othello uses the phrase sarcastically, hinting that he suspects Iago
The phrase is a title given to the ensign in the Venetian army
Everyone trusts Iago's honesty, while the audience knows he is the liar
questions.explanation: Othello, Cassio and Desdemona all call Iago honest. Each time, the audience feels the irony, which drives the theme of appearance and reality.

questions.stem: How does the play explore reputation?
options: Cassio is distraught at losing his good name, while Iago destroys others' names
Iago values reputation highly and holds to that view throughout the play
Cassio dismisses reputation as an idle and false imposition
Desdemona's good name is untouched, so the theme is limited to men
questions.explanation: Cassio cries that he has lost 'the immortal part of myself'. Iago tells him reputation is worthless, then tells Othello the opposite, 'Who steals my purse steals trash', using whichever view suits him.

questions.stem: In Act 4, Scene 3, Emilia argues that wives have 'sense like them'. What idea does her speech raise?
options: Wives should forgive their husbands' faults patiently, as Desdemona does
Women are naturally purer than men, so infidelity is a male vice
Unfaithful wives deserve whatever punishment their husbands choose
Women have the same feelings as men, and husbands who wrong them share the blame
questions.explanation: Emilia tells Desdemona that wives see, smell and taste as husbands do, and learn their faults from them. Her frank view contrasts with Desdemona's gentle innocence just before the murder.

questions.stem: How does Othello's view of himself change under Iago's influence?
options: He comes to trust Desdemona more and Iago less, until the final scene
He starts to see himself through Venetian prejudice and doubts he could be loved
He grows more confident of his place in Venice as the play goes on
He begins to believe Cassio is a better soldier and gives him his command
questions.explanation: Thinking Desdemona false, he says 'Haply, for I am black' and lists reasons she might reject him. Iago succeeds partly by turning society's prejudice into Othello's self-doubt.

questions.stem: What is the effect of Iago's soliloquies and asides?
options: The audience learns Desdemona's private feelings about Othello
The audience learns Iago's one true motive, stated clearly
The audience knows his plans and watches his victims trust him
The audience is kept as unsure of his plans as the characters are
questions.explanation: Iago confides in the audience more than Othello does, almost making us accomplices. The result is constant dramatic irony: we see the trap closing and cannot warn anyone.

questions.stem: What does the handkerchief come to symbolise?
options: Brabantio's blessing on the marriage, and then his curse
Othello's love and trust, and then false proof of betrayal
Desdemona's carelessness, and then her real betrayal of Othello
Cassio's love for Desdemona, and then his shame at losing it
questions.explanation: It was Othello's first gift, which he says an Egyptian gave his mother. When Iago passes it to Cassio, a small object becomes 'proof' that destroys a marriage.

questions.stem: In Act 4, Scene 1, Othello's speech breaks into fragmented prose before he falls into a fit. What does this show?
options: Iago's poison has destroyed the control and eloquence Othello once had
Othello is pretending to be ill so that he can escape from Lodovico
Othello is mocking Iago by copying his blunt, plain way of speaking
Othello has grown humbler, so he speaks plainly instead of in verse
questions.explanation: Early in the play Othello speaks in rich, flowing verse. His broken words before the fit show his mind collapsing, and Iago coolly says his 'medicine' is working.

questions.stem: Why does it matter that most of the play moves from Venice to Cyprus?
options: Cyprus is Desdemona's birthplace, so she has allies there to protect her
Cyprus is an isolated military outpost, far from the law and order of Venice
Cyprus is Othello's homeland, so he feels safer there than he did in Venice
Cyprus is under siege, so the soldiers must stay on constant alert
questions.explanation: In Venice the Senate hears both sides and judges fairly. On Cyprus, cut off and with the war suddenly over, there is no such check, and Iago can work unseen.

questions.stem: Iago often uses animal imagery. What is its effect?
options: It praises Othello's strength by comparing him to noble creatures
It reduces love and people to something bestial and degrading
It reflects Othello's view of love as wild and passionate
It adds comic relief to ease the tension between tragic scenes
questions.explanation: From the first scene Iago describes Othello and the marriage in crude animal terms. Later Othello too speaks of goats and monkeys, a sign that Iago's language has infected him.

questions.stem: Who says 'I am not what I am.'?
options: Emilia, as she speaks out at the end
Iago, to Roderigo in the first scene
Othello, to the Senate in Act 1
Cassio, after he loses his place
questions.explanation: In Act 1, Scene 1, Iago tells Roderigo that his outward service hides his true purpose. The line warns the audience from the start that his 'honesty' is an act.

questions.stem: Othello says, 'She loved me for the dangers I had passed, / And I loved her that she did pity them.' What does this reveal?
options: Their love grew from his promises of wealth and high rank
Their love rests on pity alone, which shows that it is shallow
Their love grew from her response to the stories of his life
Their marriage was arranged by Brabantio for political gain
questions.explanation: Answering the charge of witchcraft in Act 1, Scene 3, Othello says that 'This only is the witchcraft I have used.' His dignified story wins over the Duke.

questions.stem: When Iago warns, 'O, beware, my lord, of jealousy! / It is the green-eyed monster', what is ironic?
options: He is testing Othello's trust and hopes to be proved wrong
He is warning Othello about Roderigo's love for Desdemona
He warns Othello against the very feeling he is deliberately stirring up
He is jealous of Cassio himself and is trying to confess to Othello
questions.explanation: In Act 3, Scene 3, Iago seems to be a loyal friend giving good advice. In fact the warning plants the idea, and it makes Iago look trustworthy while he does it.

questions.stem: Iago says, 'Trifles light as air / Are to the jealous confirmations strong / As proofs of holy writ.' What is he planning?
options: To make Othello swear an oath on the Bible that he trusts his wife
To persuade Cassio that Othello has stopped suspecting Desdemona
To return the handkerchief before Desdemona notices it is gone
To use the handkerchief as proof, knowing a jealous man will believe it
questions.explanation: He says this in soliloquy in Act 3, Scene 3, just after Emilia gives him the handkerchief. Jealousy, he knows, makes small things seem as certain as scripture.

questions.stem: In his final speech Othello asks to be described as one 'that loved not wisely, but too well'. How might you respond to this?
options: It shows that he still does not know that Iago deceived him about Cassio
It is spoken by Lodovico, who wants to protect Othello's reputation
It shows his nobility returning, but it can also seem to excuse a murder
It is addressed to Desdemona's body, asking her for forgiveness
questions.explanation: The speech recovers Othello's eloquence and dignity. Yet critics differ: some see true tragic recognition, others a man shaping his own reputation even now.

questions.stem: For the question 'How does Shakespeare's Othello explore the destructive power of jealousy?', which is the strongest thesis?
options: Othello is a tragedy by William Shakespeare about a general who marries a Venetian woman
This essay will discuss the ways jealousy is explored in the play Othello by Shakespeare
In Othello there are many jealous characters, such as Othello, Iago, Roderigo and Bianca
Shakespeare shows jealousy as a poison that Iago plants, which turns Othello's trust into violence
questions.explanation: A strong thesis answers the question with an arguable claim and points to the method, here the image of poison. The others retell, announce or list without arguing.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Iago tells Othello to beware of jealousy.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List the other things Iago says to Othello in the same scene, one after another
Describe what Othello does in the next scene and in the scene after that
Explain how the warning makes Iago seem loyal while it plants the very suspicion he names
Add the act and scene and say where Othello and Iago are standing at the time
questions.explanation: Analysis explains how the evidence works. Showing the irony of the warning links it to the themes of deception and jealousy.
